text.p: Here are the highlights from Swiss newspapers on Monday:

- Headed by professor Jean Francois Bergier, the independent expert commission investigating Switzerland's role during World War Two held its first constituent meeting on Saturday in Berne. The commission will first look into the gold transactions between Switzerland and Nazi Germany.

- The Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed an article by the 'Sonntags Blick', according to which Federal Prosecutor Clara Del Ponte wants to register all owners of the so-called Natel D Easy, a smart card system used to operate cellular phones anonymously. This phone system is said to be very popular among criminals.
- Greenpeace activists blocked the railway tacks from a Swiss nuclear power plant on Sunday to halt a shipment of used nuclear fuel rods.

- Otto Stich, former finance minister and prominent Social Democrat, rejects the idea of the foundation for solidarity, which was announced last week by the Swiss government and the National Bank and will use gold reserves to finance assistance to victims of poverty, human rights abuses and the Holocaust - Some 2,000 pro-Tibet activists demonstrated against alleged Chinese violations of human rights in Tibet in front of the UN building in Geneva. The annual conference of the human rights commission starts today in Geneva.

- Three weekend opinion polls showed Swiss voters back the huge new humanitarian fund despite right-wing opposition to efforts to appease critics of Switzerland's role during World War Two. -- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
